
# Payroll and Pensions {#sec-payroll}

A State Water Resources Department pays about nine hundred employees every month. Salaries are usually the largest expenditure of such a department, larger than all its purchases. After retirement the State pays them a pension, often for twenty or thirty years, and then a family pension to the spouse. So one wrong entry in a master is repeated every month, sometimes for decades. A clerk who never existed draws a salary in one office. A pensioner who died years ago is still paid, because nobody asked for the life certificate. Each shows only when the payroll is read against another record.

Earlier chapters already hold many payroll and pension tests, such as the pay bill rule book of @sec-validate and the pensioners found dead in @sec-linkage. This chapter runs them together for one department, in a few lines each. It then adds what the book lacks. These are a review of **changes in the employee master**, a check of the payroll against **sanctioned strength** and **attendance**, and a set of **pension tests**. Finally it combines the flags for each employee and pensioner, and follows two cases to the end.

As in every chapter of this part, a flag is not a finding. Many flags in payroll have an innocent cause, such as leave, deputation or an order entered late. The aim is to find the few that need a question.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Where payroll and pensions go wrong {#sec-payroll-cycle}

Pay and pension pass through a few records, and each can be checked against the others.

| Record | What it holds | What can go wrong |
|------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Employee master | Who is employed, where, in which cadre, from when and until when | Ghost employees, leavers left on the rolls, wrong dates of birth |
| Change log of the master | Every change of pay or bank account, with the order and the user | Pay raised without an order, bank account changed to divert a payment |
| Monthly payroll | Pay, allowances, deductions and the account credited | Pay outside service, wrong allowances, the same salary paid twice |
| Sanctioned strength | The number of posts of each cadre in each office | More people paid than there are posts |
| Attendance | Days present and on leave, each month | People paid who never attend |
| Pension master and payments | Pensioners, their pension, life certificates and commutation | Pension after death, pension above the rules, the same payment twice |

: Records of payroll and pensions, and what can go wrong {#tbl-payroll-records}

The controls are simple. Nobody should be paid unless the person exists, holds a sanctioned post, is in service that month and is paid at a rate an order allows. A pensioner should be paid only while alive, and only what the rules give.

## Our data, the payroll and pensions of a State water resources department {#sec-payroll-data}

Our auditee is an imaginary Water Resources Department of a State, with a head office and eight division offices. We have its payroll and pension records for 2024-25. All names and numbers are made up. There are thirteen tables.

- `employees` is the employee master, with dates of birth, joining and leaving, PAN, bank account and mobile number.
- `master_changes` is its change log. It records each change of basic pay or bank account, with the order number and the user.
- `payroll` has one row per employee per month. It holds the days paid, basic pay, dearness allowance (DA), house rent allowance (HRA), other allowances, deductions, net pay and the account credited.
- `arrears` holds the supplementary bills for arrears, with the period covered.
- `sanctioned` holds the posts of each cadre in each office, and `attendance` a monthly summary of days present and on leave.
- `pensioners` is the pension master, with the pension payment order (PPO) number, type of pension, last pay, monthly pension and any date of death. A family pension carries the PPO of the pension it follows, in `linked_ppo`.
- `pension_paid` holds the monthly payments, `life_certs` the life certificates and `commutation` the lump sums paid on commuting part of a pension.
- `bank_salary` and `treasury_pension` hold monthly totals from the bank and the treasury.
- `oap` is the welfare department's old age pension list.

Pay follows a few example norms. DA is 50% of basic pay up to September 2024 and 53% from October 2024. HRA is 30%, 20% or 10% of basic pay in cities of class X, Y and Z. A service pension is half of the last pay drawn, and a family pension 30% of it, with a minimum of ₹9,000. Employees retire at the end of the month in which they reach 60. These are illustrative rules for this example only. In real work, apply the actual rules and rates of your government.

Most of the data is routine. Employees join mid-month and leave. Some increments were entered late and paid as arrears. A few employees were on long leave, and two engineers are on deputation to the head office. Some pensioners died and their spouses draw a family pension. A few pensioners are over a hundred, and some sent their life certificates late. Into this, these cases have been planted.

1. **Paid after leaving.** A clerk of the Motinagar office who resigned on 31 August 2024 is paid for two more months.
2. **Paid before joining.** A Junior Engineer who joined at Amarpur in January 2025 is paid for December 2024 too.
3. **A pay rise with no order.** A clerk of Dhaulagarh has basic pay raised by more than a fifth, and the change log shows no order.
4. **Two increments in a year.** A senior clerk of Belkheda receives a second annual increment in January.
5. **Arrears paid twice.** The same arrears bill of one employee is paid again two months later.
6. **A bank change just before arrears.** An accountant's account is changed four days before an arrears payment, and changed back ten days after it.
7. **Ghost employees.** Three clerks of Lakhanpur are paid every month but never attend. They share one mobile number.
8. **A very old pensioner without a life certificate.** A pensioner over 100 years old is paid all year, though his last life certificate is from 2021.
9. **Family pension and service pension together.** A pensioner died in July 2024. His widow is paid a family pension, and his own pension continues too.
10. **Commutation paid twice**, and **a pension well above the rule.**

The tests of earlier chapters will find a few more. Let us build the data.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the payroll and pension data"
set.seed(2425)

fy_start <- as.Date("2024-04-01")
fy_end   <- as.Date("2025-03-31")
fy_months <- seq(fy_start, by = "month", length.out = 12)
month_end <- function(m) ceiling_date(m, "month") - 1

offices <- tibble(
  office     = c("Head Office", "Amarpur", "Belkheda", "Chandanpur", "Dhaulagarh",
                 "Kesargaon", "Lakhanpur", "Motinagar", "Sonpur"),
  city_class = c("X", "Y", "Z", "Y", "Z", "Z", "Y", "Z", "Y"))

cadres <- tribble(
  ~cadre,                ~level, ~min_pay, ~max_pay, ~div, ~ho,
  "Executive Engineer",  11,     67700,    208700,   1,    3,
  "Assistant Engineer",  10,     56100,    177500,   4,    6,
  "Junior Engineer",      6,     35400,    112400,   20,   0,
  "Accountant",           6,     35400,    112400,   3,    8,
  "Senior Clerk",         4,     25500,     81100,   8,    20,
  "Clerk",                2,     19900,     63200,   22,   36,
  "Driver",               2,     19900,     63200,   5,    8,
  "Multi-tasking staff",  1,     18000,     56900,   30,   24,
  "Gauge Reader",         1,     18000,     56900,   16,   0)

# ---- Names ----
male   <- c("Ramesh", "Suresh", "Mahesh", "Dinesh", "Rajendra", "Surendra", "Mukesh", "Rakesh",
            "Anil", "Sunil", "Vijay", "Ajay", "Sanjay", "Manoj", "Pramod", "Vinod", "Ashok",
            "Arvind", "Deepak", "Pankaj", "Rahul", "Amit", "Sumit", "Rohit", "Naveen", "Praveen",
            "Gopal", "Govind", "Kishore", "Hemant", "Yogesh", "Satish", "Harish", "Girish",
            "Shyam", "Mohan", "Ram Prakash", "Ram Kishore", "Jagdish", "Om Prakash", "Bhagwan Das",
            "Kailash", "Laxman", "Bharat", "Shankar", "Prem", "Devendra", "Narendra", "Lalit")
female <- c("Sunita", "Anita", "Kavita", "Savita", "Geeta", "Seema", "Rekha", "Asha", "Usha",
            "Meena", "Neha", "Pooja", "Priya", "Sarita", "Kiran", "Manju", "Anju", "Rita",
            "Shanti", "Kamla", "Vimla", "Sushila", "Pushpa", "Lalita", "Radha", "Sharda",
            "Kusum", "Saroj", "Nirmala", "Shobha", "Archana", "Vandana", "Rashmi", "Jyoti")
surname <- c("Sharma", "Verma", "Gupta", "Yadav", "Singh", "Patel", "Tiwari", "Mishra", "Pandey",
             "Chauhan", "Rathore", "Joshi", "Saxena", "Shukla", "Dubey", "Meena", "Jain",
             "Agrawal", "Srivastava", "Kushwaha", "Sahu", "Rajput", "Thakur", "Soni", "Bairwa",
             "Prajapati", "Choudhary", "Bhatt", "Trivedi", "Dwivedi", "Nayak", "Malviya")
make_name <- function(g) paste(if_else(g == "M", sample(male, length(g), TRUE),
                                       sample(female, length(g), TRUE)),
                               sample(surname, length(g), TRUE))
make_pan <- function(nm) paste0(map_chr(nm, \(x) paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = "")),
                                "P", str_sub(word(nm, -1), 1, 1),
                                sprintf("%04d", sample(1:9999, length(nm), TRUE)),
                                sample(LETTERS, length(nm), TRUE))
make_acct   <- function(n) sprintf("%011.0f", runif(n, 1e10, 9.99e10))
make_mobile <- function(n) paste0(sample(6:9, n, TRUE), sprintf("%09.0f", runif(n, 1e8, 9.99e8)))
retire_on <- function(dob) rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1))

# ---- Sanctioned strength ----
sanctioned <- expand_grid(office = offices$office, cadre = cadres$cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres, by = "cadre") |>
  mutate(sanctioned = if_else(office == "Head Office", ho, div)) |>
  filter(sanctioned > 0) |>
  select(office, cadre, sanctioned)

# ---- Staff on the rolls on 1 April 2024 ----
filled <- sanctioned |>
  mutate(vacant = rbinom(n(), sanctioned, 0.08),
         vacant = case_when(office == "Lakhanpur" & cadre == "Clerk" ~ 0L,
                            office == "Head Office" & cadre == "Assistant Engineer" ~ 0L,
                            office == "Amarpur" & cadre == "Junior Engineer" ~ pmax(vacant, 2L),
                            TRUE ~ vacant),
         n = sanctioned - vacant)
staff <- filled |>
  uncount(n) |>
  select(office, cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres |> select(cadre, level, min_pay, max_pay), by = "cadre")
n0 <- nrow(staff)
staff <- staff |>
  mutate(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), n0, TRUE, prob = c(0.72, 0.28)),
         dob = fy_start - round(runif(n0, 23, 59.9) * 365.25),
         doj = pmin(dob + round(runif(n0, 21, 33) * 365.25), fy_start - sample(30:500, n0, TRUE)),
         dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)
# Retirements in the year
r <- retire_on(staff$dob) <= fy_end
staff$dol[r] <- retire_on(staff$dob[r]); staff$leave_reason[r] <- "Retirement"
# Other leavers
others <- sample(which(!r & staff$office != "Lakhanpur"), 17)
staff$leave_reason[others] <- rep(c("Resignation", "Death", "Transfer out"), c(8, 3, 6))
staff$dol[others] <- fy_start + sample(20:340, 17)
# Planted. A clerk of Motinagar resigned on 31 August 2024 (paid two more months, below)
e_left <- sample(which(staff$office == "Motinagar" & staff$cadre == "Clerk" & is.na(staff$dol)), 1)
staff$dol[e_left] <- as.Date("2024-08-31"); staff$leave_reason[e_left] <- "Resignation"
# Planted. A senior clerk of Kesargaon reached 60 in August 2024; the master was never updated
e_super <- sample(which(staff$office == "Kesargaon" & staff$cadre == "Senior Clerk" & is.na(staff$dol)), 1)
staff$dob[e_super] <- as.Date("1964-08-20"); staff$doj[e_super] <- as.Date("1990-02-12")
staff$gender[e_super] <- "M"

# New joinees during the year, into vacant posts
vac <- filled |> filter(vacant > 0, !(office == "Head Office" & cadre == "Assistant Engineer"),
                        cadre %in% c("Junior Engineer", "Clerk", "Multi-tasking staff", "Gauge Reader",
                                     "Assistant Engineer"))
joiners <- vac |>
  slice_sample(n = 26, weight_by = vacant) |>
  select(office, cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres |> select(cadre, level, min_pay, max_pay), by = "cadre") |>
  mutate(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), n(), TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
         doj = fy_start + sample(10:330, n(), TRUE),
         dob = doj - round(runif(n(), 22, 30) * 365.25),
         dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)
# Planted. A Junior Engineer of Amarpur joined on 6 January 2025 (paid for December too, below)
joiners <- bind_rows(joiners, tibble(office = "Amarpur", cadre = "Junior Engineer", level = 6,
                                     min_pay = 35400, max_pay = 112400, gender = "M",
                                     doj = as.Date("2025-01-06"), dob = as.Date("1999-05-17"),
                                     dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_))
# One Assistant Engineer awaiting posting, held at Head Office
joiners <- bind_rows(joiners, tibble(office = "Head Office", cadre = "Assistant Engineer", level = 10,
                                     min_pay = 56100, max_pay = 177500, gender = "F",
                                     doj = as.Date("2024-09-16"), dob = as.Date("1996-02-03"),
                                     dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_))
# Planted. Three clerks of Lakhanpur who do not exist
ghosts <- tibble(office = "Lakhanpur", cadre = "Clerk", level = 2, min_pay = 19900, max_pay = 63200,
                 gender = c("M", "M", "F"),
                 doj = as.Date(c("2022-08-01", "2022-11-14", "2023-03-06")),
                 dob = as.Date(c("1993-04-11", "1995-09-23", "1996-12-02")),
                 dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)

emp <- bind_rows(staff, joiners, ghosts) |>
  mutate(emp_name = make_name(gender))
ne <- nrow(emp)
emp <- emp |>
  mutate(emp_code = sprintf("%06d", sample(1000:99999, ne)),
         pan = make_pan(emp_name),
         bank_account = make_acct(ne),
         mobile = make_mobile(ne),
         yrs = pmax(0, floor(as.numeric(fy_start - doj) / 365.25)),
         basic0 = pmin(round(min_pay * 1.03^yrs, -2), max_pay))
g_idx <- (ne - 2):ne
e_join <- which(emp$doj == as.Date("2025-01-06"))
emp$basic0[g_idx] <- c(21100, 20500, 20500)
# Ghosts share one mobile number, and the third is paid into a real clerk's account
emp$mobile[g_idx] <- "9812047736"
dealer <- sample(which(emp$office == "Lakhanpur" & emp$cadre == "Clerk" & is.na(emp$dol) &
                         emp$doj < as.Date("2020-01-01")), 1)
emp$bank_account[ne] <- emp$bank_account[dealer]
# Two married couples share a mobile number (innocent)
pool <- which(is.na(emp$dol) & !seq_len(ne) %in% c(g_idx, dealer))
cp <- c(rbind(sample(intersect(pool, which(emp$gender == "M")), 2),
              sample(intersect(pool, which(emp$gender == "F")), 2)))
emp$mobile[cp[c(2, 4)]] <- emp$mobile[cp[c(1, 3)]]
emp$emp_name[cp[c(2, 4)]] <- paste(word(emp$emp_name[cp[c(2, 4)]], 1, -2), word(emp$emp_name[cp[c(1, 3)]], -1))
# Two Junior Engineers on deputation to a project cell at Head Office, where there is no JE post
dep <- c(sample(which(emp$office == "Sonpur" & emp$cadre == "Junior Engineer" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1),
         sample(which(emp$office == "Dhaulagarh" & emp$cadre == "Junior Engineer" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1))
emp$office[dep] <- "Head Office"
# Planted. Two PANs in a wrong format, and one driver paid above the scale
bad_pan <- sample(which(is.na(emp$dol) & !seq_len(ne) %in% g_idx), 2)
emp$pan[bad_pan] <- c(str_sub(emp$pan[bad_pan[1]], 1, 9), str_replace(emp$pan[bad_pan[2]], "^(.{5})", "\\1O"))
emp$pan[bad_pan[2]] <- str_sub(emp$pan[bad_pan[2]], 1, 10)
e_scale <- sample(which(emp$office == "Head Office" & emp$cadre == "Driver" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1)
emp$basic0[e_scale] <- 66400

# ---- Change log of pay ----
inc <- emp |>
  mutate(i = row_number()) |>
  filter(doj <= as.Date("2024-01-01"), is.na(dol) | dol >= as.Date("2024-07-01")) |>
  transmute(i, type = "Increment", factor = 1.03, effective = as.Date("2024-07-01"),
            entered_on = as.Date("2024-07-01") + sample(1:12, n(), TRUE))
late_inc <- sample(setdiff(inc$i, c(g_idx, e_super)), 12)
inc$entered_on[inc$i %in% late_inc] <- as.Date("2024-10-01") + sample(2:20, 12, TRUE)
# Financial upgradations (MACP) for some, five of them entered late
macp_i <- sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < as.Date("2012-01-01")),
                         c(g_idx, late_inc, e_super, e_scale, dep)), 16)
macp <- tibble(i = macp_i, type = "Financial upgradation", factor = 1.05,
               effective = sample(seq(as.Date("2024-08-01"), by = "month", length.out = 6), 16, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(entered_on = effective + sample(3:15, 16, TRUE))
macp$effective[1:5] <- as.Date(c("2024-08-01", "2024-08-01", "2024-09-01", "2024-10-01", "2024-10-01"))
macp$entered_on[1:5] <- macp$effective[1:5] %m+% months(sample(2:3, 5, TRUE)) + sample(1:15, 5, TRUE)
e_dup_arr <- macp$i[1]
# Planted. An accountant of Chandanpur, upgradation from April entered only in January
e_bank <- sample(which(emp$office == "Chandanpur" & emp$cadre == "Accountant" & is.na(emp$dol) &
                         !seq_len(ne) %in% c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan)), 1)
macp <- bind_rows(macp, tibble(i = e_bank, type = "Financial upgradation", factor = 1.12,
                               effective = as.Date("2024-04-01"), entered_on = as.Date("2025-01-08")))
# Planted. A senior clerk of Belkheda given a second increment in January
e_twice <- sample(which(emp$office == "Belkheda" & emp$cadre == "Senior Clerk" &
                          seq_len(ne) %in% setdiff(inc$i, c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan))), 1)
# Planted. A clerk of Dhaulagarh whose pay was raised with no order
e_jump <- sample(which(emp$office == "Dhaulagarh" & emp$cadre == "Clerk" &
                         seq_len(ne) %in% setdiff(inc$i, c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan))), 1)
extra <- tibble(i = c(e_twice, e_jump), type = c("Increment", "Pay fixation"), factor = c(1.03, 1.22),
                effective = as.Date(c("2025-01-01", "2024-11-01")),
                entered_on = as.Date(c("2025-01-04", "2024-11-12")))
changes <- bind_rows(inc, macp, extra) |>
  mutate(paid_from = pmax(effective, floor_date(entered_on, "month")))

# Pay due and pay drawn, month by month
grid <- expand_grid(i = seq_len(ne), month = fy_months)
due_f <- grid |> left_join(changes, by = "i", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  summarise(f_due  = prod(if_else(!is.na(effective) & effective <= month, factor, 1)),
            f_paid = prod(if_else(!is.na(paid_from) & paid_from <= month, factor, 1)),
            .by = c(i, month))
da_rate <- function(m) if_else(m >= as.Date("2024-10-01"), 0.53, 0.50)
pay_grid <- due_f |>
  mutate(basic_due  = round(emp$basic0[i] * f_due, -2),
         basic_paid = round(emp$basic0[i] * f_paid, -2))

# Log entries, with values before and after
changes <- changes |>
  mutate(new_value = pay_grid$basic_due[match(paste(i, effective), paste(pay_grid$i, pay_grid$month))],
         old_value = if_else(effective == fy_start, emp$basic0[i] / factor,
                             pay_grid$basic_due[match(paste(i, effective %m-% months(1)),
                                                      paste(pay_grid$i, pay_grid$month))]),
         old_value = round(old_value, -2))
seq_ref <- function(prefix, n) sprintf("%s/24-25/%04d", prefix, sample(1:9999, n))
pay_log <- changes |>
  mutate(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], field = "basic_pay",
         order_ref = case_when(type == "Increment" ~ seq_ref("INC", n()),
                               type == "Financial upgradation" ~ seq_ref("MACP", n()),
                               TRUE ~ NA_character_),
         entered_by = if_else(i == e_jump, "DEO-07",
                              sample(sprintf("DEO-%02d", 1:6), n(), TRUE)))

# ---- Arrears ----
arr <- pay_grid |>
  filter(basic_due > basic_paid) |>
  inner_join(changes |> filter(paid_from > effective) |> select(i, type, entered_on), by = "i") |>
  summarise(period_from = min(month), period_to = max(month),
            amount = round(sum((basic_due - basic_paid) * (1 + da_rate(month)))),
            .by = c(i, type, entered_on)) |>
  mutate(arrear_type = paste(type, "arrears"),
         paid_on = entered_on + sample(6:12, n(), TRUE))
arr$paid_on[arr$i == e_bank] <- as.Date("2025-01-17")
# Planted. One arrears bill paid twice
dup_row <- arr |> filter(i == e_dup_arr) |> mutate(paid_on = paid_on + 56)
arr <- bind_rows(arr, dup_row)
# Genuine arrears of transport allowance after a late order for drivers (innocent noise)
ta_arr <- tibble(i = which(emp$cadre == "Driver" & is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < fy_start),
                 type = "x", entered_on = as.Date("2024-12-10"), period_from = as.Date("2024-04-01"),
                 period_to = as.Date("2024-11-01"), amount = 8 * 600,
                 arrear_type = "Transport allowance arrears", paid_on = as.Date("2024-12-18"))
arr <- bind_rows(arr, ta_arr) |>
  filter(paid_on <= fy_end) |>
  arrange(paid_on, i)

# ---- Bank account changes ----
bchg <- tibble(i = sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol)), c(g_idx, dealer, e_bank)), 22),
               changed_on = fy_start + sample(5:350, 22, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(new_value = make_acct(n()))
# Planted. The Chandanpur accountant's account changed four days before the arrears, and back after
temp_acct <- make_acct(1)
bchg <- bind_rows(bchg, tibble(i = e_bank, changed_on = as.Date(c("2025-01-13", "2025-01-27")),
                               new_value = c(temp_acct, emp$bank_account[e_bank])))
bchg <- bchg |> arrange(i, changed_on) |>
  mutate(old_value = lag(new_value, default = NA), .by = i) |>
  mutate(old_value = coalesce(old_value, emp$bank_account[i]))
acct_on <- function(k, d) {
  map2_chr(k, d, \(kk, dd) {
    ch <- bchg[bchg$i == kk & bchg$changed_on <= dd, ]
    if (nrow(ch) == 0) emp$bank_account[kk] else ch$new_value[nrow(ch)]
  })
}
emp_final_acct <- acct_on(seq_len(ne), fy_end)
arr <- arr |> mutate(paid_to_account = acct_on(i, paid_on))

# ---- Monthly payroll ----
hra_rate <- c(X = 0.30, Y = 0.20, Z = 0.10)
on_roll <- grid |>
  mutate(m_end = month_end(month), start = emp$doj[i], stop = coalesce(emp$dol[i], fy_end),
         days = as.numeric(pmin(m_end, stop) - pmax(month, start)) + 1,
         frac = pmin(1, days / as.numeric(m_end - month + 1))) |>
  filter(days > 0)
# Planted. Paid after leaving (Motinagar) and before joining (Amarpur)
on_roll <- bind_rows(on_roll,
                     tibble(i = e_left, month = as.Date(c("2024-09-01", "2024-10-01")), frac = 1),
                     tibble(i = e_join, month = as.Date("2024-12-01"), frac = 1))
# The Kesargaon senior clerk stays on the rolls all year (no date of leaving in the master)
payroll <- on_roll |>
  select(i, month, frac) |>
  left_join(pay_grid |> select(i, month, basic_paid), by = c("i", "month")) |>
  mutate(office = emp$office[i], level = emp$level[i],
         city_class = offices$city_class[match(office, offices$office)],
         days_paid = round(frac * days_in_month(month)),
         basic_pay = round(basic_paid * frac),
         da_pct = da_rate(month),
         # Planted. Sonpur pays the new DA rate two months early
         da_pct = if_else(office == "Sonpur" & month %in% as.Date(c("2024-08-01", "2024-09-01")), 0.53, da_pct),
         da = round(da_pct * basic_pay),
         hra = round(hra_rate[city_class] * basic_pay),
         other_allow = round(case_when(level >= 9 ~ 7200, level >= 3 ~ 3600, TRUE ~ 1800) * frac),
         gross = basic_pay + da + hra + other_allow,
         deductions = round(0.10 * (basic_pay + da)) + 200 + round(pmax(0, gross - 90000) * 0.10),
         net_pay = gross - deductions,
         pay_date = month_end(month),
         bank_account = acct_on(i, pay_date),
         emp_code = emp$emp_code[i])
# Planted. A person not in the master, paid by Belkheda from January
stranger <- payroll |> filter(office == "Belkheda", level == 1, month >= as.Date("2025-01-01")) |>
  filter(i == i[1]) |>
  mutate(emp_code = "070815", bank_account = make_acct(1))
# Planted. One January salary at Sonpur paid twice
dup_sal <- payroll |> filter(office == "Sonpur", month == as.Date("2025-01-01")) |> slice_sample(n = 1)
payroll <- bind_rows(payroll, stranger, dup_sal) |>
  arrange(month, office, emp_code) |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, days_paid, basic_pay, da, hra, other_allow, gross, deductions, net_pay,
         pay_date, bank_account)

# ---- Attendance summary ----
long_leave <- tibble(i = sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < fy_start),
                                        c(g_idx, dealer, e_super, e_bank, e_jump, e_twice, e_scale, e_left,
                                          bad_pan, cp, dep, e_dup_arr, late_inc)), 5),
                     from = sample(fy_months[2:7], 5, TRUE), len = sample(3:5, 5, TRUE))
attendance <- on_roll |>
  filter(!i %in% g_idx,
         !(i == e_left & month > as.Date("2024-08-01")),
         !(i == e_join & month < as.Date("2025-01-01")),
         !(i == e_super & month > as.Date("2024-08-01"))) |>
  left_join(long_leave, by = "i") |>
  filter(is.na(from) | month < from | month >= from %m+% months(len)) |>
  mutate(working = 26 - (wday(month_end(month)) == 1),
         days_leave = sample(0:3, n(), TRUE, prob = c(5, 3, 2, 1)),
         days_present = pmax(0, round(working * frac) - days_leave),
         emp_code = as.numeric(emp$emp_code[i])) |>
  select(emp_code, month, days_present, days_leave)

# ---- Employee master, at 31 March 2025 ----
employees <- emp |>
  mutate(bank_account = emp_final_acct) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, gender, cadre, office, dob, doj, dol, leave_reason, pan, bank_account, mobile) |>
  arrange(emp_code)
master_changes <- bind_rows(
  pay_log |> transmute(emp_code, field, change_type = type, old_value = as.character(old_value),
                       new_value = as.character(new_value), effective_from = effective,
                       order_ref, entered_on, entered_by),
  bchg |> transmute(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], field = "bank_account", change_type = "Bank details",
                    old_value, new_value, effective_from = changed_on,
                    order_ref = NA_character_, entered_on = changed_on,
                    entered_by = if_else(i == e_bank, "DEO-03", sample(sprintf("DEO-%02d", 1:6), n(), TRUE)))
) |> arrange(entered_on, emp_code)
arrears <- arr |>
  mutate(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], bill_no = sprintf("SB/%04d", sample(1000:9999, n()))) |>
  select(emp_code, arrear_type, period_from, period_to, amount, bill_no, paid_on, paid_to_account)

bank_salary <- bind_rows(payroll |> transmute(month = floor_date(pay_date, "month"), amount = net_pay),
                         arrears |> transmute(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), amount)) |>
  summarise(bank_debits = sum(amount), .by = month) |> arrange(month)

# ---- Pensions ----
np <- 1250
pen <- tibble(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), np, TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2)),
              age = 60.1 + 38 * rbeta(np, 1, 2.6)) |>
  mutate(dob = fy_start - round(age * 365.25))
# Genuine pensioners over 100, and one planted
pen <- bind_rows(pen, tibble(gender = c("M", "F", "M", "M", "M"),
                             dob = as.Date(c("1922-08-14", "1923-01-30", "1924-02-19", "1921-11-05",
                                             "1920-06-14"))))
np <- nrow(pen)
pen <- pen |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender), pension_type = "Service", linked_ppo = NA_character_,
         retirement_date = retire_on(dob), pension_start = retirement_date + 1,
         last_pay = round(sample(c(18000, 19900, 25500, 35400, 56100, 67700), np, TRUE,
                                 prob = c(5, 6, 4, 4, 2, 1)) * runif(np, 1.2, 2.3), -2),
         share = if_else(runif(np) < 0.06, runif(np, 0.30, 0.48), 0.5),
         monthly_pension = pmax(round(share * last_pay), 9000))
# New pensioners, the employees who retired during the year
newp <- emp |>
  mutate(i = row_number()) |>
  filter(leave_reason %in% "Retirement") |>
  left_join(pay_grid |> filter(month == as.Date("2025-03-01")) |> select(i, basic_due), by = "i") |>
  transmute(gender, dob, name = emp_name, pension_type = "Service", linked_ppo = NA_character_,
            retirement_date = dol, pension_start = dol + 1, last_pay = basic_due, share = 0.5,
            monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.5 * last_pay), 9000)) |>
  filter(pension_start <= fy_end)
pen <- bind_rows(pen, newp)
# Existing family pensioners
nf <- 290
famold <- tibble(gender = sample(c("F", "M"), nf, TRUE, prob = c(0.92, 0.08)),
                 dob = fy_start - round(runif(nf, 52, 94) * 365.25)) |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender), pension_type = "Family",
         linked_ppo = if_else(runif(nf) < 0.7, sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(1:8000, nf)), NA_character_),
         retirement_date = as.Date(NA),
         pension_start = fy_start - sample(200:9000, nf, TRUE),
         last_pay = round(sample(c(18000, 19900, 25500, 35400, 56100), nf, TRUE) * runif(nf, 1.2, 2.2), -2),
         share = 0.3, monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.3 * last_pay), 9000))
pen <- bind_rows(pen, famold) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(8001:29999, n())),
         date_of_death = as.Date(NA))
# Planted. One pension far above the rule
p_high <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$share == 0.5 & pen$last_pay > 60000 &
                         pen$pension_start < fy_start), 1)
pen$monthly_pension[p_high] <- round(0.78 * pen$last_pay[p_high])
p_old <- which(pen$dob == as.Date("1920-06-14"))
# Deaths of pensioners in the year. Most leave a spouse, who gets a family pension
dead <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$pension_start < fy_start &
                       pen$dob > as.Date("1925-01-01") & seq_len(nrow(pen)) != p_high), 14,
               prob = as.numeric(fy_start - pen$dob[pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$pension_start < fy_start &
                                                     pen$dob > as.Date("1925-01-01") &
                                                     seq_len(nrow(pen)) != p_high])^3)
pen$date_of_death[dead] <- fy_start + sample(10:300, 14)
dm <- dead[pen$gender[dead] == "M"][1]
dead <- c(dm, setdiff(dead, dm))
p_both <- dead[1]
pen$date_of_death[p_both] <- as.Date("2024-07-19")
spouse <- pen[dead[1:9], ] |>
  transmute(gender = if_else(gender == "M", "F", "M"),
            dob = dob + round(runif(9, 2, 7) * 365.25),
            name = paste(if_else(gender == "F", sample(female, 9, TRUE), sample(male, 9, TRUE)), word(name, -1)),
            pension_type = "Family", linked_ppo = ppo_no, retirement_date = as.Date(NA),
            pension_start = floor_date(date_of_death, "month") %m+% months(1),
            last_pay, share = 0.3, monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.3 * last_pay), 9000),
            ppo_no = sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(30001:30999, 9)), date_of_death = as.Date(NA))
pen <- bind_rows(pen, spouse) |>
  mutate(bank_account = make_acct(n()))
nP <- nrow(pen)

# Monthly pension payments
pension_paid <- expand_grid(k = seq_len(nP), month = fy_months) |>
  filter(pen$pension_start[k] <= month_end(month),
         is.na(pen$date_of_death[k]) | month <= floor_date(pen$date_of_death[k], "month") |
           k == p_both) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = pen$ppo_no[k], amount = pen$monthly_pension[k], paid_on = month_end(month)) |>
  select(ppo_no, month, paid_on, amount)

# Commutation for the new pensioners, paid once each, and once twice (planted)
commutation <- pen |>
  filter(pension_type == "Service", pension_start >= fy_start) |>
  transmute(ppo_no, paid_on = pension_start + sample(30:75, n(), TRUE),
            amount = round(0.4 * monthly_pension * 12 * 8.194)) |>
  filter(paid_on <= fy_end)
p_comm <- commutation$ppo_no[2]
commutation <- bind_rows(commutation,
                         commutation |> filter(ppo_no == p_comm) |> mutate(paid_on = paid_on + 97)) |>
  arrange(paid_on) |>
  mutate(bill_no = sprintf("CB/%04d", sample(1000:9999, n())))

# Life certificates
lc <- pen |> mutate(k = row_number()) |>
  filter(pension_start < as.Date("2024-11-01"))
cert_day <- function(n, yr) as.Date(paste0(yr, "-11-01")) + round(rnorm(n, 12, 9))
life_certs <- bind_rows(
  lc |> filter(pension_start < as.Date("2023-11-01")) |> transmute(k, cert_date = cert_day(n(), 2023)),
  lc |> transmute(k, cert_date = cert_day(n(), 2024))
) |>
  filter(is.na(pen$date_of_death[k]) | cert_date < pen$date_of_death[k])
# Late certificates (innocent but a lapse): the 2024 certificate came in January or February
late_lc <- sample(setdiff(lc$k[lc$pension_start < as.Date("2023-06-01") & is.na(pen$date_of_death[lc$k])],
                          c(p_old, p_high)), 11)
life_certs <- life_certs |>
  mutate(cert_date = if_else(k %in% late_lc & cert_date >= as.Date("2024-09-01"),
                             as.Date("2025-01-04") + sample(0:50, n(), TRUE), cert_date),
         cert_date = if_else(k %in% late_lc & cert_date < as.Date("2024-01-01"),
                             as.Date("2023-11-01") + sample(0:6, n(), TRUE), cert_date))
# Planted. The oldest pensioner's last certificate is from November 2021
life_certs <- life_certs |> filter(k != p_old) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(k = p_old, cert_date = as.Date("2021-11-18"))) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = pen$ppo_no[k]) |>
  arrange(ppo_no, cert_date) |>
  select(ppo_no, cert_date)

pensioners <- pen |>
  select(ppo_no, name, gender, dob, pension_type, linked_ppo, retirement_date, pension_start,
         last_pay, monthly_pension, date_of_death, bank_account) |>
  arrange(ppo_no)
treasury_pension <- bind_rows(pension_paid |> select(month, amount),
                              commutation |> transmute(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), amount)) |>
  summarise(treasury_debits = sum(amount), .by = month) |> arrange(month)

# ---- Old age pension list of the welfare department ----
no <- 900
oap <- tibble(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), no, TRUE),
              dob = fy_start - round(runif(no, 60, 92) * 365.25)) |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender))
# Planted. Two service pensioners also on the old age pension list, names written differently
twins <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & is.na(pen$date_of_death) & pen$gender == "M" &
                        pen$pension_start < fy_start & seq_len(nP) != p_old), 2)
oap <- bind_rows(oap, tibble(gender = "M", dob = pen$dob[twins],
                             name = c(str_replace(pen$name[twins[1]], "(\\w+) (\\w+)$", "\\1 Kumar \\2"),
                                      str_replace_all(pen$name[twins[2]], c("ee" = "i", "sh" = "s", "v" = "w")))))
oap <- oap |>
  slice_sample(prop = 1) |>
  mutate(oap_id = sprintf("OAP-%04d", row_number()),
         district = sample(c("North", "South", "East", "West"), n(), TRUE),
         monthly_pension = 1000) |>
  select(oap_id, name, gender, dob, district, monthly_pension)
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("employees", "master_changes", "payroll", "arrears", "sanctioned",
                          "attendance", "pensioners", "pension_paid", "life_certs", "commutation",
                          "bank_salary", "treasury_pension", "oap")))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
lakh <- function(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)
crore <- function(x) round(x / 1e7, 2)
inr <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(round(x))
  vapply(s, function(v) {
    n <- nchar(v)
    if (n <= 3) return(v)
    head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(v, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
    paste0(head, ",", substr(v, n - 2, n))
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
fdate <- function(d) sub("^0", "", format(d, "%d %B %Y"))
fmonth <- function(d) format(d, "%B %Y")
ename <- function(code) employees$emp_name[match(code, employees$emp_code)]
pname <- function(ppo) pensioners$name[match(ppo, pensioners$ppo_no)]
words <- c("no", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
num <- function(n) if (n <= 10) words[n + 1] else as.character(n)
```

Let us look at the main tables.

```{r}
glimpse(employees)
glimpse(master_changes)
glimpse(payroll)
glimpse(pensioners)
glimpse(pension_paid)
```

Two keys link the tables. `emp_code` links the employee master to the change log, payroll, arrears and attendance. `ppo_no` links the pension master to the payments, certificates and commutation. Every test below is a join along one of these links.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, the data to request

Ask for the whole year, in raw form. For pay, that is the employee master with its **change log**, the monthly payroll with the account credited, the arrears bills, the sanctioned strength and the attendance summary. For pensions, it is the pension master, the monthly payments, the life certificate register and the commutation payments. The change log matters most. The current master shows only the last value, and hides a change made and then reversed. Ask also for the bank's and treasury's monthly totals. Note who ran each extract and when.
:::

## First, is the data complete? {#sec-payroll-complete}

A test on incomplete data proves nothing. @sec-recon reconciled records item by item. Here a quicker check is enough. First, the keys of the two masters must be unique.

```{r}
c(employees  = anyDuplicated(employees$emp_code),
  pensioners = anyDuplicated(pensioners$ppo_no))
```

`anyDuplicated()` returns 0 when nothing is repeated. Next, every employee paid should be in the master. `anti_join()` keeps the rows with no partner.

```{r}
payroll |>
  anti_join(employees, by = "emp_code") |>
  count(emp_code, office)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
stranger <- payroll |> anti_join(employees, by = "emp_code")
```

One code, `r stranger$emp_code[1]`, is paid by the `r stranger$office[1]` office for `r num(nrow(stranger))` months, but is not in the master. We note it, and come back to it in @sec-payroll-earlier. Finally, the salaries and arrears in our data should add up to what the bank paid out, month by month.

```{r}
arrears_by_month <- arrears |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month")) |>
  summarise(arrears = sum(amount), .by = month)

payroll |>
  summarise(salaries = sum(net_pay), .by = month) |>
  left_join(arrears_by_month, by = "month") |>
  mutate(arrears = coalesce(arrears, 0)) |>
  left_join(bank_salary, by = "month") |>
  mutate(difference = salaries + arrears - bank_debits) |>
  print(n = 12)
```

`coalesce()` turns a missing arrears total into 0, for months with no arrears bill. Every month agrees. The year's salaries come to ₹`r crore(sum(payroll$net_pay))` crore in `r big(nrow(payroll))` monthly payments, and arrears to ₹`r lakh(sum(arrears$amount))` lakh. The same check works for pensions.

```{r}
pension_paid |>
  summarise(pension = sum(amount), .by = month) |>
  left_join(commutation |>
              mutate(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month")) |>
              summarise(commuted = sum(amount), .by = month),
            by = "month") |>
  left_join(treasury_pension, by = "month") |>
  summarise(difference = sum(pension + coalesce(commuted, 0) - treasury_debits))
```

This agrees too. Pensions of ₹`r crore(sum(pension_paid$amount))` crore were paid to `r big(n_distinct(pension_paid$ppo_no))` pensioners in the year. In real work, a difference here is the first thing to settle.

## Changes in the employee master {#sec-payroll-master}

The employee master decides who is paid and how much, and its change log shows how that changed. So we start here.

### Paid before joining or after leaving {#sec-payroll-service}

An employee may be paid only for the days in service. So a salary for a month that ends before the date of joining, or begins after the date of leaving, is wrong. Leaving covers resignation, retirement, death and transfer.

```{r}
outside <- payroll |>
  inner_join(employees |> select(emp_code, doj, dol, leave_reason), by = "emp_code") |>
  mutate(month_end = ceiling_date(month, "month") - 1) |>
  filter(month_end < doj | (!is.na(dol) & month > dol))

outside |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, days_paid, doj, dol, leave_reason, net_pay)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
left_case <- outside |> filter(!is.na(dol))
join_case <- outside |> filter(is.na(dol))
mid_joiners <- payroll |>
  inner_join(employees |> select(emp_code, doj), by = "emp_code") |>
  filter(doj >= as.Date("2024-04-02"), floor_date(doj, "month") == month)
```

`ceiling_date(month, "month") - 1` gives the last day of the month. Employee `r left_case$emp_code[1]` of `r left_case$office[1]` resigned on `r fdate(left_case$dol[1])`, but was paid for `r paste(format(left_case$month, "%B"), collapse = " and ")`, ₹`r inr(sum(left_case$net_pay))` in all. Employee `r join_case$emp_code[1]` of `r join_case$office[1]` joined on `r fdate(join_case$doj[1])`, but was paid in full for `r fmonth(join_case$month[1])`. The `r nrow(mid_joiners)` other joinees of the year were paid from the day they joined, and rightly do not appear.

Each test of this chapter ends by keeping the codes of the flagged employees in an object whose name starts with `f_`, for flag. We combine them all in @sec-payroll-risk.

```{r}
f_outside <- unique(outside$emp_code)
```

### Pay raised without an order {#sec-payroll-rise}

Basic pay rises with an increment, a promotion or an upgradation, and each needs an order. So every rise in the payroll should have an entry in the change log, with an order number, entered before the salary was paid. Let us first find the rises, month on month. Months paid in part are left out, since their pay is lower for that reason alone.

```{r}
rises <- payroll |>
  arrange(emp_code, month) |>
  mutate(full = days_paid == days_in_month(month),
         prev_basic = lag(basic_pay), prev_full = lag(full), prev_date = lag(pay_date),
         .by = emp_code) |>
  filter(full, prev_full, basic_pay > prev_basic)
nrow(rises)
```

`lag()` gives the value of the row before, here within each employee. There are `r big(nrow(rises))` rises, nearly all of them the increment of July. Now we look for an entry in the change log with an order, entered after the previous month's salary and on or before this month's. An inequality join does this.

```{r}
pay_log <- master_changes |>
  filter(field == "basic_pay", !is.na(order_ref))

backed <- rises |>
  semi_join(pay_log, by = join_by(emp_code, prev_date < entered_on, pay_date >= entered_on))

no_order <- rises |>
  anti_join(backed, by = c("emp_code", "month"))
no_order |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, prev_basic, basic_pay)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
jump <- no_order[1, ]
jump_log <- master_changes |> filter(emp_code == jump$emp_code, field == "basic_pay")
jump_fix <- jump_log |> filter(is.na(order_ref))
late_entries <- master_changes |>
  filter(field == "basic_pay", effective_from < floor_date(entered_on, "month"))
```

We match on the date of entry, not the date of effect. An increment due in July but entered in October shows in the October payroll. All `r nrow(late_entries)` such late entries are matched. One rise is not. Let us read that employee's log.

```{r}
master_changes |>
  filter(emp_code == jump$emp_code) |>
  select(change_type, old_value, new_value, effective_from, order_ref, entered_on, entered_by)
```

The basic pay of employee `r jump$emp_code`, a clerk of `r jump$office`, was raised from ₹`r inr(jump$prev_basic)` to ₹`r inr(jump$basic_pay)` in `r fmonth(jump$month)`, a rise of `r round(100 * (jump$basic_pay / jump$prev_basic - 1))`%. The log calls it a "`r jump_fix$change_type`", with no order number, entered by user `r jump_fix$entered_by`. A pay fixation needs an order too. The rise costs about ₹`r inr((jump$basic_pay - jump$prev_basic) * 1.53)` a month in pay and DA alone.

```{r}
f_rise <- unique(no_order$emp_code)
```

### More than one increment in a year {#sec-payroll-increment}

In our example, an employee earns one increment a year. Let us count the pay changes of each employee.

```{r}
pay_changes <- master_changes |>
  filter(field == "basic_pay")

pay_changes |>
  count(emp_code, name = "changes") |>
  count(changes, name = "employees")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pc <- pay_changes |> count(emp_code, name = "changes")
two_inc <- pay_changes |> filter(change_type == "Increment") |> filter(n() > 1, .by = emp_code)
```

`r sum(pc$changes > 1)` employees had two changes. Most had an increment and an upgradation, which is normal. So we count increments alone.

```{r}
pay_changes |>
  filter(change_type == "Increment") |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = emp_code) |>
  select(emp_code, old_value, new_value, effective_from, order_ref, entered_by)
```

One employee, `r two_inc$emp_code[1]`, a `r str_to_lower(employees$cadre[employees$emp_code == two_inc$emp_code[1]])` of `r employees$office[employees$emp_code == two_inc$emp_code[1]]`, received an increment on `r fdate(two_inc$effective_from[1])` and another on `r fdate(two_inc$effective_from[2])`. Both carry order numbers, so the last test did not catch it. Some rules allow a second increment, for example as an incentive. The second order must say which rule.

```{r}
f_twoinc <- unique(two_inc$emp_code)
```

### Bank account changed around an arrears payment {#sec-payroll-bank}

@sec-pay-bankchange showed a vendor's account changed for a few days to divert one payment. The same can be done to an employee. A salary is a poor target, since the employee would notice. A one-time payment such as arrears is a better one.

```{r}
bank_log <- master_changes |>
  filter(field == "bank_account") |>
  select(emp_code, old_value, new_value, entered_on, entered_by)
nrow(bank_log)
```

Changes of account are normal. Two patterns are not. The first is a change that is **reversed** soon after. We join the log to itself, as in @sec-pay-bankchange.

```{r}
reversed <- bank_log |>
  inner_join(bank_log |> select(emp_code, back_on = entered_on, back_to = new_value),
             by = join_by(emp_code, old_value == back_to, entered_on < back_on)) |>
  mutate(days_held = as.numeric(back_on - entered_on))
reversed |>
  select(emp_code, entered_on, back_on, days_held, entered_by)
```

The second is an **arrears payment soon after a change**. We join each arrears bill to any change in the 15 days before it.

```{r}
after_change <- arrears |>
  inner_join(bank_log |> mutate(window_end = entered_on + 15),
             by = join_by(emp_code, between(paid_on, entered_on, window_end))) |>
  mutate(days_after = as.numeric(paid_on - entered_on))
after_change |>
  select(emp_code, arrear_type, period_from, period_to, amount, entered_on, paid_on, days_after)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bk <- after_change[1, ]
bk_net <- median(payroll$net_pay[payroll$emp_code == bk$emp_code])
bk_temp <- reversed$new_value[1]
bk_other <- c(sum(employees$bank_account == bk_temp), sum(payroll$bank_account == bk_temp),
              sum(arrears$paid_to_account == bk_temp))
bk_user <- master_changes |> filter(entered_by == reversed$entered_by[1], field == "bank_account")
```

The two patterns point at the same person. Employee `r bk$emp_code`, an accountant of `r employees$office[employees$emp_code == bk$emp_code]`, had the account changed on `r fdate(reversed$entered_on[1])`. Arrears of ₹`r inr(bk$amount)` for `r fmonth(bk$period_from)` to `r fmonth(bk$period_to)` were paid on `r fdate(bk$paid_on)`, `r num(bk$days_after)` days later, into the new account. The employee's usual net pay is about ₹`r inr(bk_net)` a month. `r if (bk$amount == max(arrears$amount)) "This was the largest arrears bill of the year." else ""` On `r fdate(reversed$back_on[1])` the old account was put back. Both changes were made by user `r reversed$entered_by[1]`. `r if (sum(bk_other) == 1) "The new account appears nowhere else in our data. It received this one payment and nothing more." else "The new account appears elsewhere in our data too."` The upgradation has an order. The question is whether the employee received the money.

```{r}
f_bank <- unique(c(reversed$emp_code, after_change$emp_code))
```

### Arrears paid twice {#sec-payroll-arrears}

Arrears are paid by a supplementary bill. Two bills for the same employee, kind of arrears and period are a duplicate, as in @sec-dup.

```{r}
arrears_twice <- arrears |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(emp_code, arrear_type, period_from, period_to))
arrears_twice |>
  select(emp_code, arrear_type, period_from, period_to, amount, bill_no, paid_on)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
at <- arrears_twice
```

Employee `r at$emp_code[1]` was paid `r str_to_lower(at$arrear_type[1])` of ₹`r inr(at$amount[1])` for `r fmonth(at$period_from[1])` to `r fmonth(at$period_to[1])` twice, by bills `r at$bill_no[1]` and `r at$bill_no[2]`, on `r fdate(at$paid_on[1])` and `r fdate(at$paid_on[2])`. The amount is small, but a system that pays arrears twice will do so for large amounts too. The `r nrow(filter(arrears, arrear_type == "Transport allowance arrears"))` bills of transport allowance arrears for drivers share a period and amount. Each is for a different driver, so the test rightly leaves them alone.

```{r}
f_arrears <- unique(arrears_twice$emp_code)
```

## Payroll against sanctioned strength {#sec-payroll-strength}

Every post is sanctioned by an order, for each office and cadre. An office may have vacant posts. It should not pay more people than it has posts. Let us count the employees paid in each office and cadre each month, and take the largest count.

```{r}
paid_strength <- payroll |>
  inner_join(employees |> select(emp_code, cadre), by = "emp_code") |>
  summarise(paid = n_distinct(emp_code), .by = c(office, cadre, month)) |>
  summarise(max_paid = max(paid), .by = c(office, cadre))

strength_check <- paid_strength |>
  left_join(sanctioned, by = c("office", "cadre")) |>
  mutate(excess = max_paid - sanctioned)

strength_check |>
  filter(is.na(sanctioned) | excess > 0)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
over <- strength_check |> filter(excess > 0)
lak <- over |> filter(office == "Lakhanpur")
ho_ae <- over |> filter(office == "Head Office")
no_post <- strength_check |> filter(is.na(sanctioned))
no_post_emp <- employees |> semi_join(no_post, by = c("office", "cadre"))
```

Three rows stand out. Lakhanpur paid up to `r lak$max_paid` clerks against `r lak$sanctioned` sanctioned posts, `r num(lak$excess)` more than it may. The Head Office paid `r ho_ae$max_paid` Assistant Engineers against `r ho_ae$sanctioned` posts. The extra one joined in September and awaits posting, a common and temporary reason. The third row has no sanctioned post at all. The Head Office pays `r num(nrow(no_post_emp))` Junior Engineers, the two on deputation, against no post of that cadre. The order should name the posts they are borne against. For now we flag every employee of these groups.

```{r}
f_nopost <- no_post_emp$emp_code
f_excess <- employees |>
  semi_join(filter(strength_check, excess > 0), by = c("office", "cadre")) |>
  pull(emp_code)
```

This test works on counts. It says that Lakhanpur has three clerks too many, but not which three. For that we need a second record of each person.

## Payroll against attendance {#sec-payroll-attendance}

A real employee leaves a trail of attendance and leave. A ghost leaves only a salary. So an employee paid for a month with no attendance record at all needs a look. Let us join the payroll with the attendance summary.

```{r}
glimpse(attendance)

payroll |>
  semi_join(attendance |> mutate(emp_code = as.character(emp_code)), by = "emp_code") |>
  nrow()
```

No row matches. The `glimpse()` shows why. The attendance file stores the employee code as a number, so the code `r sprintf('%06d', attendance$emp_code[1])` became `r as.character(attendance$emp_code[1])`. This is the problem of lost leading zeros of @sec-strng-zeros. We pad the codes back to six digits with `str_pad()`.

```{r}
attendance <- attendance |>
  mutate(emp_code = str_pad(as.character(emp_code), width = 6, pad = "0"))
```

Now the months paid with no attendance record at all.

```{r}
no_record <- payroll |>
  anti_join(attendance, by = c("emp_code", "month")) |>
  summarise(months_no_record = n_distinct(month), .by = c(emp_code, office)) |>
  left_join(payroll |> summarise(months_paid = n_distinct(month), .by = emp_code), by = "emp_code") |>
  left_join(employees |> select(emp_code, cadre, mobile), by = "emp_code") |>
  arrange(desc(months_no_record))
no_record
```

```{r}
#| include: false
all_months <- no_record |> filter(months_no_record == months_paid)
ghost_codes <- all_months |> filter(!is.na(cadre)) |> pull(emp_code)
some_months <- no_record |> filter(months_no_record < months_paid)
super_code <- employees |>
  filter(is.na(dol), rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1)) < as.Date("2025-03-31")) |>
  pull(emp_code)
leave_codes <- setdiff(some_months$emp_code, c(f_outside, super_code))
```

`r nrow(no_record)` codes were paid for at least one month with no record. They fall into three groups.

- **No record in any month.** `r str_to_sentence(num(length(ghost_codes)))` clerks of `r unique(all_months$office[all_months$emp_code %in% ghost_codes])` were paid in all `r all_months$months_paid[all_months$emp_code == ghost_codes[1]]` months and never marked present or on leave. They share one mobile number. With them is the code `r stranger$emp_code[1]`, which is not in the master at all.
- **A few months with no record, explained by our other tests.** The clerk paid after resigning and the engineer paid before joining appear for those months. A senior clerk of Kesargaon, `r super_code`, has no record for `r no_record$months_no_record[no_record$emp_code == super_code]` months. We see why in @sec-payroll-earlier.
- **A few months with no record, and nothing else wrong.** `r str_to_sentence(num(length(leave_codes)))` employees have runs of `r min(no_record$months_no_record[no_record$emp_code %in% leave_codes])` to `r max(no_record$months_no_record[no_record$emp_code %in% leave_codes])` months with no record, in the middle of the year. This is the pattern of long leave sanctioned by a higher office and never entered in the attendance system. The leave orders will show.

```{r}
f_noatt_all <- all_months$emp_code
f_noatt_some <- some_months$emp_code
```

::: callout-warning
## Caution, many flags have innocent causes

A missing attendance record may mean long leave, deputation, training or a late entry. A pay rise without an order may be an order not yet entered. A count above the posts may be an officer awaiting posting. So treat every flag as a question to the office. Ask for the leave, deputation or relieving order before calling anything an irregularity. An office that cannot produce the papers for many flags has a weak control, even when no money is lost.
:::

## Pensions {#sec-payroll-pensions}

Pensions are paid for decades, often by a treasury or a bank, and nobody sees the pensioner each month. The main control is the yearly **life certificate**, by which the pensioner proves that he or she is alive. When it fails, a pension may run on long after death.

```{r}
pensioners |>
  count(pension_type)
```

### Pensioners of a great age {#sec-payroll-age}

A pensioner over 100 is rare but possible. Such a pensioner should have a recent life certificate. Let us find the living pensioners aged 100 or more on 31 March 2025, with their latest certificate. `interval()` and `time_length()` give the age in completed years, as in @sec-lubridate.

```{r}
last_cert <- life_certs |>
  summarise(last_cert = max(cert_date), .by = ppo_no)

very_old <- pensioners |>
  filter(is.na(date_of_death)) |>
  mutate(age = floor(time_length(interval(dob, as.Date("2025-03-31")), "years"))) |>
  filter(age >= 100) |>
  left_join(last_cert, by = "ppo_no")
very_old |>
  select(ppo_no, name, age, pension_type, monthly_pension, last_cert)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
old_bad <- very_old |> filter(last_cert < as.Date("2024-01-01"))
old_ok <- very_old |> filter(last_cert >= as.Date("2024-01-01"))
```

`r str_to_sentence(num(nrow(very_old)))` living pensioners are 100 or older. `r str_to_sentence(num(nrow(old_ok)))` of them sent a life certificate in `r paste(unique(format(old_ok$last_cert, "%B %Y")), collapse = " or ")`, and are simply very old. One is different. `r old_bad$name[1]`, `r old_bad$ppo_no[1]`, is `r old_bad$age[1]` years old, and his last life certificate is dated `r fdate(old_bad$last_cert[1])`.

```{r}
f_old <- old_bad$ppo_no
```

### Pension paid after the life certificate expired {#sec-payroll-lifecert}

Let us test every payment. In our example norm, a life certificate is valid until the end of the same month a year later. A new pensioner needs none in the first year, so the start of the pension also counts as a check. For each payment we need the latest check on or before it. This is a rolling join with `closest()`, as for the rate in force in @sec-joins-audit.

```{r}
checks <- bind_rows(life_certs,
                    pensioners |> transmute(ppo_no, cert_date = pension_start))

expired <- pension_paid |>
  left_join(checks, by = join_by(ppo_no, closest(paid_on >= cert_date))) |>
  mutate(valid_till = rollforward(cert_date %m+% years(1))) |>
  filter(paid_on > valid_till)

expired_by_ppo <- expired |>
  summarise(months = n(), amount = sum(amount), last_check = max(cert_date), .by = ppo_no) |>
  arrange(desc(months))
expired_by_ppo
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ex_old <- expired_by_ppo |> filter(ppo_no %in% f_old)
dead_ppo <- pensioners$ppo_no[!is.na(pensioners$date_of_death) & pensioners$ppo_no %in% expired_by_ppo$ppo_no]
ex_dead <- expired_by_ppo |> filter(ppo_no %in% dead_ppo)
ex_late <- expired_by_ppo |> filter(!ppo_no %in% c(f_old, dead_ppo))
late_next <- life_certs |>
  semi_join(ex_late, by = "ppo_no") |>
  filter(cert_date >= as.Date("2024-06-01"))
```

`rollforward()` moves a date to the end of its month. `r nrow(expired_by_ppo)` pensioners were paid at least once on an expired certificate. The planted pensioner over 100 heads the list, with all `r ex_old$months` months of the year, ₹`r lakh(ex_old$amount)` lakh. The next, `r ex_dead$ppo_no[1]`, was paid for `r ex_dead$months[1]` months on an expired certificate. That pensioner died in `r fmonth(pensioners$date_of_death[pensioners$ppo_no == ex_dead$ppo_no[1]])`, so no new certificate could come. We meet him again in the next section. The other `r nrow(ex_late)` were paid for `r min(ex_late$months)` or `r max(ex_late$months)` months each. Their new certificates came in later, between `r fdate(min(late_next$cert_date))` and `r fdate(max(late_next$cert_date))`. The pensioners were alive, but the payments were made without the check. That lapse is worth reporting as a pattern.

```{r}
f_expired <- expired_by_ppo$ppo_no
```

### Family pension and service pension together {#sec-payroll-family}

When a pensioner dies, the pension stops, and the spouse may get a family pension from the next month. The two should never be paid for the same month. We join each family pension to the payments of its `linked_ppo` from the month it started.

```{r}
both_paid <- pensioners |>
  filter(pension_type == "Family", !is.na(linked_ppo)) |>
  select(family_ppo = ppo_no, linked_ppo, family_start = pension_start) |>
  inner_join(pension_paid, by = join_by(linked_ppo == ppo_no, family_start <= month))

both_paid |>
  summarise(months = n(), amount = sum(amount), from = min(month), to = max(month),
            .by = c(family_ppo, linked_ppo))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bp <- both_paid |> summarise(months = n(), amount = sum(amount), from = min(month), to = max(month),
                             .by = c(family_ppo, linked_ppo))
bp_dead <- pensioners |> filter(ppo_no == bp$linked_ppo[1])
n_family_new <- pensioners |> filter(pension_type == "Family", pension_start >= as.Date("2024-04-01")) |> nrow()
```

Of the `r n_family_new` family pensions that began during the year, one overlaps. `r bp_dead$name`, `r bp_dead$ppo_no`, died on `r fdate(bp_dead$date_of_death)`. His widow's family pension, `r bp$family_ppo[1]`, began in `r fmonth(bp$from[1])`, yet his own pension was paid every month from `r fmonth(bp$from[1])` to `r fmonth(bp$to[1])`, ₹`r lakh(bp$amount[1])` lakh. The office that sanctioned the family pension knew of the death, but the service pension was never stopped. A simpler test needs no family pension. Any payment for a month after a recorded death is wrong.

```{r}
pension_paid |>
  inner_join(pensioners |> filter(!is.na(date_of_death)) |> select(ppo_no, date_of_death), by = "ppo_no") |>
  filter(month > floor_date(date_of_death, "month")) |>
  count(ppo_no, date_of_death, name = "months_after_death")
```

The same pensioner appears. Where a death is not recorded at all, link the list with the death register, as @sec-linkage did.

```{r}
f_both <- unique(c(bp$family_ppo, bp$linked_ppo))
```

### Commutation paid twice {#sec-payroll-commutation}

On retirement, a pensioner may **commute** part of the pension, taking a lump sum once in return for a smaller pension for some years. Our monthly payments leave out the reduction, for simplicity. Let us look for a PPO paid more than once.

```{r}
commutation |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = ppo_no)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
cm <- commutation |> filter(n() > 1, .by = ppo_no)
```

`r pname(cm$ppo_no[1])`, `r cm$ppo_no[1]`, was paid a commutation of ₹`r lakh(cm$amount[1])` lakh on `r fdate(cm$paid_on[1])`, and again on `r fdate(cm$paid_on[2])`, by a different bill. Of `r n_distinct(commutation$ppo_no)` commutations paid in the year, this is the only repeat. It is also the largest single overpayment in this chapter.

```{r}
f_comm <- unique(cm$ppo_no)
```

### Pension against a simple rule {#sec-payroll-rule}

A pension depends on the last pay and the length of service, under detailed rules that the auditor should apply as they stand. For a first screen, a simple rule shows the cases far off the mark. Our illustrative rule is the one stated with the data. A pension below it may be correct, since short service gives less. A pension well above it needs a look.

```{r}
pension_rule <- pensioners |>
  mutate(rule_share = if_else(pension_type == "Service", 0.5, 0.3),
         by_rule = pmax(round(rule_share * last_pay), 9000),
         ratio = round(monthly_pension / by_rule, 2))

pension_rule |>
  count(above = ratio > 1.05, below = ratio < 0.95)

pension_rule |>
  filter(ratio > 1.05) |>
  select(ppo_no, name, pension_type, last_pay, monthly_pension, by_rule, ratio)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
hi <- pension_rule |> filter(ratio > 1.05)
hi_paid <- sum(pension_paid$amount[pension_paid$ppo_no == hi$ppo_no[1]])
hi_excess <- (hi$monthly_pension[1] - hi$by_rule[1]) * sum(pension_paid$ppo_no == hi$ppo_no[1])
```

`r sum(pension_rule$ratio < 0.95)` pensions are below the rule, which short service explains. One is above it. `r hi$name[1]`, `r hi$ppo_no[1]`, draws ₹`r inr(hi$monthly_pension[1])` a month, against ₹`r inr(hi$by_rule[1])` by the rule, `r hi$ratio[1]` times as much. If the rule holds, the excess for this year alone is ₹`r lakh(hi_excess)` lakh. A pension fixed wrongly is paid wrongly for life. Ask for the pension papers and work it out under the real rules.

```{r}
f_rule <- hi$ppo_no
```

### The same person on two pension lists {#sec-payroll-twolists}

Under many schemes, a service pensioner may not also draw an old age pension, as in @sec-privacy-data. The two lists have no common key, so we link them as in @sec-linkage. We block on date of birth and gender, and compare names with the Jaro-Winkler distance of @sec-strsim.

```{r}
std_name <- function(x) str_squish(str_to_lower(str_remove_all(x, "[^A-Za-z ]")))

candidates <- pensioners |>
  filter(pension_type == "Service", is.na(date_of_death)) |>
  select(ppo_no, name, gender, dob) |>
  inner_join(oap |> select(oap_id, oap_name = name, gender, dob), by = c("gender", "dob"),
             relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(jw = round(stringdist(std_name(name), std_name(oap_name), method = "jw", p = 0.1), 3)) |>
  arrange(jw)
nrow(candidates)
head(candidates, 5)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
twin <- candidates |> filter(jw < 0.15)
next_jw <- candidates |> filter(jw >= 0.15) |> slice(1)
```

A person on one list may share a date of birth with several on the other, so we tell `inner_join()` to expect a many-to-many relationship. `r nrow(candidates)` pairs share a date of birth and gender. Two pairs have very close names, `r paste0(twin$name, " and ", twin$oap_name, collapse = ", and ")`, with distances of `r paste(twin$jw, collapse = " and ")`. The next pair, `r next_jw$name` and `r next_jw$oap_name`, is plainly two different people, at `r next_jw$jw`. A gap like this makes the cut-off easy, here 0.15. The close pairs are candidates, not findings. The welfare department should check them against its own papers before stopping either pension.

```{r}
f_twolists <- twin$ppo_no
```

::: callout-warning
## Caution, privacy of employee and pensioner data

Payroll and pension data hold names, dates of birth, PANs, bank accounts and mobile numbers of thousands of people. Use them only for the audit, keep them in a protected folder, and do not put full account numbers or PANs in the report. Use the employee codes and PPO numbers instead. Linking with another department's list needs particular care. @sec-privacy explains how to mask, pseudonymise and match lists without sharing identifiers. A name in a list of flags is not a finding against that person.
:::

## What earlier chapters add {#sec-payroll-earlier}

Several tests from earlier chapters apply directly. We run each in a few lines, and the chapters cited explain them in full.

**The pay bill rule book**, @sec-validate. We check three rules with `filter()`, as in @sec-validate-filter. The first is DA at the rate in force. A rolling join finds the rate for each month, as in @sec-nonequi and @sec-joins-audit.

```{r}
da_rates <- tibble(effective_from = as.Date(c("2024-01-01", "2024-10-01")),
                   da_pct = c(50, 53))

da_wrong <- payroll |>
  left_join(da_rates, by = join_by(closest(month >= effective_from))) |>
  filter(abs(da - da_pct / 100 * basic_pay) > 1)
da_wrong |>
  summarise(employees = n(), excess = sum(da - round(da_pct / 100 * basic_pay)), .by = c(office, month))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
daw <- da_wrong |> summarise(employees = n(), excess = sum(da - round(da_pct / 100 * basic_pay)), .by = c(office, month))
```

`r unique(daw$office)` paid DA at the new rate of 53% in `r paste(format(daw$month, "%B"), collapse = " and ")`, before it took effect, an excess of ₹`r lakh(sum(daw$excess))` lakh. This is an office-wide error, noted against the office. Next come basic pay within the range of the cadre, with example ranges, and the PAN format of @sec-regex-validate.

```{r}
pay_range <- tribble(
  ~cadre,                ~min_pay, ~max_pay,
  "Executive Engineer",  67700,    208700,
  "Assistant Engineer",  56100,    177500,
  "Junior Engineer",     35400,    112400,
  "Accountant",          35400,    112400,
  "Senior Clerk",        25500,     81100,
  "Clerk",               19900,     63200,
  "Driver",              19900,     63200,
  "Multi-tasking staff", 18000,     56900,
  "Gauge Reader",        18000,     56900)

out_of_range <- payroll |>
  filter(days_paid == days_in_month(month)) |>
  inner_join(employees |> select(emp_code, cadre), by = "emp_code") |>
  left_join(pay_range, by = "cadre") |>
  filter(basic_pay < min_pay | basic_pay > max_pay)
out_of_range |>
  summarise(months = n(), basic_pay = max(basic_pay), max_pay = max(max_pay), .by = c(emp_code, cadre))

bad_pan <- employees |>
  filter(!str_detect(pan, "^[A-Z]{3}P[A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$"))
bad_pan |>
  select(emp_code, office, pan)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
oor <- out_of_range |> summarise(months = n(), basic_pay = max(basic_pay), max_pay = max(max_pay), .by = c(emp_code, cadre))
```

A driver, `r oor$emp_code[1]`, is paid above the top of the driver's range in all `r oor$months[1]` months. `r str_to_sentence(num(nrow(bad_pan)))` PANs are in a wrong format. One is too short, and one has the letter O where a digit should be. The HRA rule passes for every row, as an exercise shows.

**Superannuation**, @sec-lubridate and @sec-validate-rules. An employee retires at the end of the month of reaching 60. A person reaches an age on the day before the birthday, so we subtract a day before rolling forward to the month end.

```{r}
past_60 <- employees |>
  mutate(superannuation = rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1))) |>
  filter(superannuation <= as.Date("2025-03-31"), is.na(dol) | dol > superannuation)
past_60 |>
  select(emp_code, office, cadre, dob, superannuation, dol)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
p60 <- past_60[1, ]
p60_paid <- payroll |> filter(emp_code == p60$emp_code, month > p60$superannuation)
n_retired <- sum(employees$leave_reason %in% "Retirement")
```

The `r n_retired` employees who retired during the year all left on the right date. One did not leave at all. Employee `r p60$emp_code`, a senior clerk of `r p60$office`, was born on `r fdate(p60$dob)` and should have retired on `r fdate(p60$superannuation)`. The master has no date of leaving, and the payroll paid ₹`r lakh(sum(p60_paid$net_pay))` lakh for the `r nrow(p60_paid)` months after. That is why the code had no attendance after August. Perhaps he was re-employed, which needs an order. Perhaps he simply went home.

**Employees not in the master.** The code `r stranger$emp_code[1]` found in @sec-payroll-complete was paid ₹`r inr(sum(stranger$net_pay))` by `r stranger$office[1]` in `r num(nrow(stranger))` months, and has no attendance either. A payroll that accepts such a code has lost its main control.

**One account, several salaries**, @sec-duckdb-tests.

```{r}
shared_acct <- payroll |>
  summarise(employees = n_distinct(emp_code), codes = paste(sort(unique(emp_code)), collapse = ", "),
            .by = c(bank_account, month)) |>
  filter(employees > 1) |>
  count(codes, name = "months")
shared_acct
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sa_codes <- str_split_1(shared_acct$codes[1], ", ")
sa_ghost <- intersect(sa_codes, ghost_codes)
sa_real <- setdiff(sa_codes, ghost_codes)
```

One account received two salaries in every month of the year. One of the two codes is `r sa_ghost`, a Lakhanpur clerk with no attendance. The other is `r sa_real`, `r ename(sa_real)`, also a clerk of Lakhanpur, who attends every month. We follow this in @sec-payroll-case-ghost.

**The same salary paid twice**, @sec-dup-exact.

```{r}
dup_salary <- payroll |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(emp_code, month))
dup_salary |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, net_pay, bank_account)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ds <- dup_salary[1, ]
```

Employee `r ds$emp_code` of `r ds$office` was paid the salary of `r fmonth(ds$month)` twice, ₹`r inr(ds$net_pay)` each time. Both reached the bank, so the completeness check could not see it.

**Ghost employees by regression**, @sec-reg-audit. That section found offices that spent more on salary than their staff explained. With only nine offices, a regression has too few points. The tests against posts and attendance do the job person by person.

**Other chapters.** The ledger entries for salaries and pensions can be tested as in @sec-jet. Each salary credit can be matched with the bank item by item, as in @sec-recon. A pension list is checked against a death register in @sec-linkage-finding.

```{r}
f_super <- p60$emp_code
f_range <- unique(out_of_range$emp_code)
f_pan <- bad_pan$emp_code
f_stranger <- unique(stranger$emp_code)
f_shared_acct <- sa_codes
f_dup <- unique(dup_salary$emp_code)
f_mobile <- employees |> filter(n() > 1, .by = mobile) |> pull(emp_code)
```

We also kept the employees who share a mobile number.

```{r}
employees |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = mobile) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, office, cadre, mobile) |>
  arrange(mobile)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
mob <- employees |> filter(n() > 1, .by = mobile) |> count(mobile)
```

`r str_to_sentence(num(nrow(mob)))` numbers are shared. Two are shared by a man and a woman with the same surname, most likely married couples, which is innocent. The third is the ghosts' number.

## A risk view of each employee and pensioner {#sec-payroll-risk}

An employee caught by one test may have a good reason. One caught by several is a better use of the auditor's time. As in @sec-tenderflags-cri and @sec-pay-risk, the simplest way to combine flags is to count them.

```{r}
emp_flags <- list(
  paid_outside_service  = f_outside,
  pay_rise_no_order     = f_rise,
  two_increments        = f_twoinc,
  bank_change_arrears   = f_bank,
  arrears_twice         = f_arrears,
  above_sanctioned      = f_excess,
  no_post_in_office     = f_nopost,
  no_attendance_ever    = f_noatt_all,
  no_attendance_some    = f_noatt_some,
  past_superannuation   = f_super,
  pay_outside_range     = f_range,
  invalid_pan           = f_pan,
  not_in_master         = f_stranger,
  shared_account        = f_shared_acct,
  same_salary_twice     = f_dup,
  shared_mobile         = f_mobile
)

emp_risk <- tibble(test = names(emp_flags), emp_code = emp_flags) |>
  unnest(emp_code) |>
  distinct() |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = emp_code) |>
  left_join(payroll |> summarise(paid = sum(net_pay), .by = emp_code), by = "emp_code") |>
  mutate(office = coalesce(employees$office[match(emp_code, employees$emp_code)], "Not in master"),
         paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(emp_code, office, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

emp_risk |>
  print(n = 10)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_emp_flag <- nrow(emp_risk)
top_emp <- emp_risk |> filter(flags >= 3)
stopifnot(setequal(top_emp$emp_code, ghost_codes))
two_codes <- emp_risk$emp_code[emp_risk$flags == 2]
stopifnot(setequal(two_codes, c(super_code, sa_real, f_outside, stranger$emp_code[1])))
n_lak_only <- sum(emp_risk$tests == "above_sanctioned" & emp_risk$office == "Lakhanpur")
n_ho_only <- sum(emp_risk$tests == "above_sanctioned" & emp_risk$office == "Head Office")
```

`tibble()` with a list column, followed by `unnest()`, turns the named list into a long table. `r n_emp_flag` of `r nrow(employees)` employees raise at least one flag. Most raise only one. `r n_lak_only` of them are Lakhanpur clerks, and `r n_ho_only` are Assistant Engineers of the Head Office, flagged only because their office pays more people of their cadre than it has posts. The top of the list is different. The `r num(nrow(top_emp))` codes with three or more flags are the three ghost clerks. Next come `r num(length(two_codes))` codes with two flags. They are the senior clerk past 60, the real clerk whose account one ghost uses, and the clerk paid after resigning. They also include the engineer paid before joining and the person not in the master. Some serious cases, such as the arrears paid during a short-lived bank change, raise only one flag. So the count orders the work. It does not decide what to ignore.

The same idea works for pensioners.

```{r}
pen_flags <- list(
  over_100_old_certificate = f_old,
  paid_on_expired_cert     = f_expired,
  family_and_service_paid  = f_both,
  commutation_twice        = f_comm,
  above_pension_rule       = f_rule,
  also_on_oap_list         = f_twolists
)

pen_risk <- tibble(test = names(pen_flags), ppo_no = pen_flags) |>
  unnest(ppo_no) |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = ppo_no) |>
  left_join(pension_paid |> summarise(paid = sum(amount), .by = ppo_no), by = "ppo_no") |>
  mutate(paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(ppo_no, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

pen_risk |>
  print(n = 6)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pen_two <- pen_risk |> filter(flags >= 2)
```

`r nrow(pen_risk)` of `r big(nrow(pensioners))` pensioners raise a flag. `r str_to_sentence(num(nrow(pen_two)))` raise two. They are the pensioner over 100 and the pensioner whose service pension ran on after his death. A count treats every test as equal, though a pension paid after death is far more serious than a late certificate. @sec-jet-score showed how to weight tests, with weights fixed before looking at the results.

::: callout-note
## A flag is a lead

None of these tests proves a fraud. Each says where to look. The work that follows is ordinary audit work, with service books, registers, people and banks. The analysis tests every employee and every month, and so points that work at the right places.
:::

## Audit use case, ghost employees in one office {#sec-payroll-case-ghost}

Let us follow the Lakhanpur clerks. We show the three codes and the real clerk, with accounts masked as in @sec-privacy-mask.

```{r}
mask <- function(x) paste0("XXXXXXX", str_sub(x, -4))

employees |>
  filter(emp_code %in% c(ghost_codes, sa_real)) |>
  mutate(account = mask(bank_account)) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, cadre, doj, mobile, account)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
gh <- employees |> filter(emp_code %in% ghost_codes)
gh_paid <- payroll |> filter(emp_code %in% ghost_codes)
real_att <- attendance |> filter(emp_code == sa_real)
lak_month <- payroll |>
  filter(office == "Lakhanpur") |>
  mutate(has_attendance = paste(emp_code, month) %in% paste(attendance$emp_code, attendance$month)) |>
  summarise(paid = n_distinct(emp_code), with_attendance = sum(has_attendance), .by = month) |>
  mutate(gap = paid - with_attendance)
other_lak <- no_record |> filter(office == "Lakhanpur", !emp_code %in% ghost_codes)
gh_inc <- master_changes |> filter(emp_code %in% ghost_codes, field == "basic_pay")
```

The story fits together. The three joined between `r fmonth(min(gh$doj))` and `r fmonth(max(gh$doj))`. They share one mobile number, which no real employee uses. One of them is paid into the account of `r ename(sa_real)`, a real clerk of the same office, present in all `r nrow(real_att)` months. Not one of the three was ever marked present or on leave. Yet they were paid ₹`r lakh(sum(gh_paid$net_pay))` lakh in the year, July increment included. Let us see the office month by month.

```{r}
payroll |>
  filter(office == "Lakhanpur") |>
  mutate(has_attendance = paste(emp_code, month) %in% paste(attendance$emp_code, attendance$month)) |>
  summarise(paid = n_distinct(emp_code), with_attendance = sum(has_attendance), .by = month) |>
  mutate(gap = paid - with_attendance) |>
  print(n = 12)
```

`r if (min(lak_month$gap) == max(lak_month$gap)) paste0("In every month, exactly ", num(min(lak_month$gap)), " of the people Lakhanpur paid had no attendance record.") else paste0("In every month, ", num(min(lak_month$gap)), " or more of the people Lakhanpur paid had no attendance record.")` `r if (nrow(other_lak) > 0) paste0("In some months the gap is larger, because ", num(nrow(other_lak)), " other employee", if (nrow(other_lak) > 1) "s were" else " was", " on long leave. ") else ""`Four records agree. The payroll pays the three, the attendance system has never seen them, the posts have no room for them, and the bank details lead to one real employee. That employee, and the clerk who prepares the pay bill, are the first people to ask.

### What the auditor does next

1. Ask for the **service books** and **appointment orders** of the three. Check them against the appointing authority's own register.
2. Check the **attendance registers** and biometric records since they joined.
3. Hold a **physical verification** of every clerk of the office, on a day fixed without notice.
4. Ask the bank, through the department, for the **holder of each account** and the KYC papers.
5. Work out the **total paid** since each joined. If confirmed, the case goes to the vigilance wing for recovery, and shows that pay bills were passed with no check against attendance or posts.

## Audit use case, pensions paid without a valid life certificate {#sec-payroll-case-lifecert}
